title: The foolishness of the cross (1 Corinthians 1:18–25)
hookLine: the foolishness of God is wiser than men

lines: A SCRATCH ON A ROMAN WALL.
cards: On the Palatine Hill in Rome, archaeologists found a drawing scratched on an ancient plaster wall. It shows a figure on a cross with the head of a donkey, and a young man raising a hand toward it.

Underneath, in rough Greek: Alexamenos worships his god. It's a joke, somebody's mockery of a Christian: worshiping a crucified man was ridiculous enough to draw. Paul would not have been surprised by it at all.

teach.b: Now to Paul's letters to Corinth, a rich, proud, quarrelsome port city. The church there is divided, and some members prize clever speech and wisdom. So Paul starts at the hardest point.
In the Douay-Rheims: "For the word of the cross, to them indeed that perish, is foolishness; but to them that are saved, that is, to us, it is the power of God."
The Greek word for foolishness is moria, folly. Yes, Paul is saying, to plenty of listeners this sounds absurd. A crucified Messiah.

teach.h: A GOD WHO WINS BY LOSING.
teach.b: A God who wins by losing. To some, a stumbling block; to others, foolishness. He doesn't make it sound more respectable.
He turns it around: "For the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men."

teach.h: NOT MANY WISE, NOT MANY MIGHTY.
teach.b: Then, with a smile, he tells the Corinthians to look at themselves: not many of you were wise by worldly standards, not many powerful, not many of noble birth. God chose what the world counts foolish and weak.

teach.h: THE FOOLISHNESS OF GOD IS WISER.
teach.b: The mocking drawing and Paul's letter agree on one thing: from the outside, the cross looks absurd. Paul's claim is that the absurd thing is exactly where God chose to show his power.
Catholic churches set a crucifix on or near the altar: the very image the mocker drew, now held up without embarrassment.

how: Catholic churches place a crucifix on or near the altar, Catholics often wear or hang one at home, and on Good Friday the faithful come forward to venerate the cross.

o: a joke told to mock someone's faith
a lack of schooling or education
folly: how the cross sounded to outsiders

p: the man mocked on a Roman wall

s: Paul tried to make the cross sound respectable
he admits it sounds foolish, then says God's foolishness is wiser than men.
an ancient drawing in Rome mocks a Christian for worshiping a crucified figure
the Alexamenos graffito on the Palatine Hill: Alexamenos worships his god.
Paul says most of the Corinthians were wise and powerful
not many wise, not many mighty, not many noble.

games.q: you're Paul. the church in Corinth prizes clever speech, and your message centers on an execution. where do you start?
o: with the cross itself, admitting how foolish it sounds.
games.why: he starts at the hardest point: the preaching of the cross is foolishness to some, but to us the power of God.

practice: Think of a kindness that looks a little silly by the world's math: letting someone have the parking spot, paying for the coffee behind you, spending time with someone who can't do anything for you, forgiving a debt.
Picture doing it, and someone shaking their head, and let that be fine. If you pray, look at a crucifix or picture one, and remember how foolish it looked.

wordCard.voice: Moria. Greek for folly: Paul's word for how the crucified Messiah sounded to the world, and the heart of what Paul would not soften. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: foolishness, folly. to some, Paul says, the word of the cross sounds like moria.

carryVoice: Your line: foolish and wise. The cross once looked like a joke on a wall. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: For the word of the cross, to them indeed that perish, is foolishness; but to them that are saved, that is, to us, it is the power of God.
For the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men.
